historical_references.reference: Saint Hadrian was a 3rd-century Roman soldier who became a Christian martyr. He is the patron saint of gardeners, travellers, and architects. According to legend, Hadrian was a soldier in the Roman army and was ordered to execute the Christian deacon Saints Symphorian and Callistus. When he refused, he was beaten and then buried alive in a barrel. Miraculously, Hadrian survived and was later released and able to live as a Christian.

Hadrian the Hagiorite was a 16th-century monk who lived in the Cave of the Syrians in Palestine. He was known for his great asceticism and was venerated as a saint. Hadrian lived in a cave near the Dead Sea and sustained himself by gathering wild herbs and eating only the fruit of a certain tree. He was also known for his miraculous abilities, including the ability to heal the sick.

modern_usage.modern_context: The Christian name 'Hadron' is derived from Greek, meaning 'that which is given'. In modern context, it is most commonly used in particle physics research, specifically in relation to subatomic particles. The name Hadron is used to describe a class of particles that are held together by the strong nuclear force. The study of hadrons is conducted through high-energy physics experiments, such as those at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, Fermilab Tevatron Collider, and in the ATLAS and CMS experiments. These experiments allow physicists to explore the fundamental nature of matter and the universe, making breakthrough discoveries like the Higgs boson.
